stem: Look at two pictures of a rock slope. In the first, the hollow at the foot of the slope is dry. In the second, the hollow is full and the rock has wet streaks. Draw the way the water went from the slope to the hollow.
answer: A route drawn down the slope and ending in the hollow, with the hollow shown holding water.
steps: draws the route starting high on the slope and ending in the hollow | shows the hollow holding water | draws the route on the slope, not only the water in the hollow
samples: An arrow runs from the top of the slope down the rock and into the hollow, and the hollow is drawn full of water. | An arrow runs from the hollow up to the top of the slope.

stem: A tray picture shows two hills, a pool in the valley, and an arrow drawn from the pool up a hill. A pour record card shows that the water ran from the hilltop down to the pool. Draw this tray the way we draw ours, with the arrow fixed from the record.
answer: Two hills, the valley pool, the arrow running from the hilltop down to the pool, and the key box filled in.
steps: draws the two hills and the valley pool | draws the arrow running from the hilltop down to the pool | fills in the key box so a partner could read the arrow
samples: Two hills with a pool between them, an arrow from the top of a hill down to the pool, and a key box that says the arrow means the water went this way. | The pool is drawn alone with an arrow pointing up a hill and no key box.

stem: A model has two hills, a river and the ocean, but no hollow. Three new pictures show rain gathering in a hollow between the hills, the water rising, and then the water running over the low edge into the river. Change the model to match the new pictures.
answer: A hollow added between the hills and holding water, with a route running from the hollow into the river, and the ocean still on the model.
steps: adds a hollow between the hills and shows water collected in it | draws the route from the hollow down into the river | keeps the ocean on the redrawn model
samples: A hollow between the hills with water in it, an arrow from the low edge of the hollow into the river, and the ocean still at the page edge. | A blue mark is added on bare paper and the ocean is rubbed out.

stem: A playground picture shows water following a low path into a dip. A tray record shows water collecting between hills. Draw this corner, and mark one thing its water did that the tray water did. Add a key box.
answer: The low path, the dip and the water collected in the low ground, with the matching mark on the tray record, both marks explained in a key.
steps: draws the low path, the dip and the water collected in the low ground | marks the thing the corner and the tray share, that the water collects in low ground | the route runs down to the dip and the marks have a key
samples: The path slopes down into the dip with water in it, a mark in the dip and the same mark between the tray hills, and a key that says the mark means the water collected. | The dip and the water are drawn alone, with no path and no key.

stem: Pip says that water always lies between hills. One page shows a pond beside a cliff. One page shows a stream between two hills. Draw the page that does not fit what Pip said.
answer: The pond page: a pond beside a cliff, with no hill on the far side of the pond.
steps: draws the pond beside the cliff, not the stream page | draws the land beside the water, the cliff and no hill on the other side
samples: A pond with a tall cliff on one side and flat ground on the other. | A stream running between two hills.

stem: One page is a map with a dotted key and a caption that puts a pond beside a hill. Another page says that ponds are lovely. Mark the pond on the page that tells where there is water.
answer: The map page, with the pond dot marked beside the hill, matched to the key (dot = pond) and the caption (A pond lies beside the hill).
steps: marks the map page, not the page that says ponds are lovely | marks the pond dot beside the hill, after matching the dot to the key
samples: Marks the round pond dot beside the hill on the map page, and points to the key to show the dot means a pond. | Marks the page about lovely ponds.

stem: Page P shows liquid brook, waterfall, rain barrel and fountain. Page Q shows solid frost, hail and glacier. Claim X says that both pages show water. Claim Y says that only page P shows water. Which claim do both pages support? Show it with a mark on each page.
answer: Claim X, with a place on page P marked and a place on page Q marked.
steps: picks claim X | marks one place on page P | marks one place on page Q
samples: Claim X, a mark on the brook of page P and a mark on the frost of page Q. | Claim Y, because only page P has water.

stem: Look at the new packet. Mark each water place liquid or solid.
answer: The pool and the stream marked liquid, the ice on the pond marked solid (it is low, not high), and the opinion page not used.
steps: marks the pool and the stream as liquid | marks the ice on the pond as solid | does not use the opinion page as a source
samples: Pool, filled mark, liquid. Stream, filled mark, liquid. Ice on the pond, open mark, solid. I did not use the opinion page. | The opinion page is marked because it is my favorite, and the ice is left off.

stem: Draw a model of the ridge, hollow and lower stream, with a key.
answer: A keyed drawing of the ridge, the hollow with the pool and the stream on lower ground, with the route running down and not over the ridge.
steps: draws the ridge and the hollow, not only the water | draws the pool and the lower stream and the route running downhill | adds a key for the marks
samples: The ridge and the hollow are drawn, the pool is in the hollow, the stream runs low and away from the ridge, and the key says what the marks mean. | Only a pool and a stream are drawn, with the stream climbing over the ridge and no key.

stem: How do you know the stream is low? Finish: I know the stream is low because ___.
answer: A reason that names the picture, the tray or the map that shows the stream on lower ground.
steps: names a route or a place | names the evidence, a picture, the tray or a page
samples: I know the stream is low because the picture shows it below the hollow and the ridge. | I know it because the teacher said so.

stem: Look at records A, B and C in your packet. Which records tell where water is in Pine Coast?
answer: Records A and B. C records another place, Other Cove.
steps: marks records A and B and leaves out record C because C records Other Cove, not Pine Coast
samples: A and B tell about Pine Coast. C is Other Cove, a different place. | I picked C because it is my favourite place.

stem: Use the records you chose to fill in your chart: for each of ocean, river, lake, pond, ice and snow, write the record it came from and whether it is liquid or solid.
answer: Ocean, river and ice from A with the key; lake, pond and snow from B. Ocean, river, lake and pond are liquid; ice and snow are solid.
steps: uses the map key of record A to read the marks of A | records the ocean, river, lake and pond in the places the records show | finds the ice in record A and the snow in record B, each with its record letter | marks the ocean, river, lake and pond as liquid and the ice and snow as solid
samples: Ocean, A, liquid. River, A, liquid. Ice, A, solid. Lake, B, liquid. Pond, B, liquid. Snow, B, solid. The filled marks on A mean liquid and the open mark means solid. | Ocean, river, lake and pond, liquid. Snow is not water, so it is left off.

stem: Say where the liquid water is and where the solid water is in Pine Coast, using your two records.
answer: In Pine Coast the liquid water is the ocean at the coast, the river, the lake and the pond. The solid water is the ice and snow on the high ridge. This is what these two records show, not a rule for every place.
steps: says where the liquid water is (ocean, river, lake, pond) and where the solid water is (the ice and snow on the ridge), for Pine Coast only
samples: In Pine Coast the liquid water is the ocean, river, lake and pond, and the ice and snow are up on the ridge. | Water is always low everywhere.

stem: In your packet are two views of one bay. Make a picture model of this area, with a key.
answer: Two rounded hills with a narrow valley between them, a bending river in the valley with its mouth in the ocean, and a key that names the marks.
steps: draws both hills and the valley with shapes that can be recognised | draws the bending river and the ocean | places the river in the valley between the hills, opening into the ocean | adds a key that tells what each mark means
samples: Two hills, a valley between them, a bending river in the valley that ends in the ocean, and a key box that says what the marks mean. | Only a river and an ocean are drawn, with no hills and no key.

stem: The caption says that rainwater runs along the valley toward the river mouth. Use your model to say why the water goes that way.
answer: The water runs along the low valley toward the river mouth, because the valley is lower than the hills.
steps: shows the water route running along the valley toward the mouth, not over the hills, and says it goes there because the valley is lower
samples: The water goes along the valley to the river mouth because the valley is lower. | The water goes up over the hills to the ocean.

stem: Say how a map could show a different area.
answer: A map of a different area would show its own hills, water and places, in the shapes and places that area has, with its own key.
steps: says a map of another area uses that area's own shapes and places
samples: A different area has its own hills and water, so its map has its own shapes in their own places. | A map of a different area looks just like this one.

stem: Look at the curb picture. Where did the water by the curb go?
answer: It ran from the higher ground down along the curb, toward the lower end, and one arrow shows that way.
steps: puts a finger on the high ground first | follows the finger downhill along the water | draws one arrow along that way | stops at the low end and draws the hollow there
samples: The finger starts on the grass and goes down along the curb to the low end, and one arrow is drawn the same way. | The finger starts at the puddle and goes up the grass.

stem: Look at the map and its key. Point to the river.
answer: The wavy band that the key calls river.
steps: looks at the key before pointing | points to the wavy band, not the hump | the support the child used is recorded on the scale: shown, shown with help, not yet seen
samples: Looks at the key, then points to the wavy band. | Points to the rounded hump.

stem: Point to the hill on the map.
answer: The rounded hump that the key calls hill.
steps: points to the rounded hump | the support the child used is recorded on the scale: shown, shown with help, not yet seen
samples: Points to the rounded hump. | Points to the wavy band.

stem: Sketch the yard after rain. Show the way the water went and the place where it stayed.
answer: High ground and a low place drawn, an arrow running down from the high ground to the low place, and the water drawn collected in the low place.
steps: draws the high ground and the low place, not only the water | draws the arrow starting high and ending low | draws the water collected in the low place
samples: A slope on the left, a hollow at its foot with water in it, and an arrow from the top of the slope down into the hollow. | Only a blue puddle, with no slope or arrow.

stem: Your partner pointed to your sketch. Redraw one thing.
answer: One thing on the sketch is changed or added, such as the slope outline, the arrow or the water in the low place.
steps: changes or adds one thing | the change answers what the partner pointing showed was missing or unclear
samples: Adds the slope outline round the puddle after the partner asked where the water came from. | Colours the sky and changes nothing about the water.

stem: Watch the tray. The sand is the land and the cup of water is the rain. Where does the water go? Draw the arrow and fill the key.
answer: Two marks of land, a hill and a low place, and one arrow running from the top of the hill down into the low place where the water stays, with the key saying what the arrow means.
steps: says the sand stands for land and the cup of water stands for rain | pours once at the top of the hill and watches where the water goes | draws the arrow from the hill top down to the low place where the water stays | draws the key box with arrow, hill, hollow and water
samples: The arrow runs from the hill top down to the low place and the key says arrow = the water went this way. | The arrow starts in the low place and runs up the hill, with no key.

stem: Before you pour, show with a finger the way the water will go.
answer: A finger route that starts at the top of a hill and runs down to the low place.
steps: the finger starts on high ground | the finger ends in the low place | the guess is said aloud as a guess
samples: The finger starts on the hilltop and slides down into the valley. | The finger starts in the valley and climbs the hill.

stem: Pour slowly from a hilltop. Draw an arrow for each way the water went.
answer: An arrow from each pour that starts at the hilltop and ends in the low place, drawn on the pour record sheet.
steps: draws only routes the group saw | each arrow starts high and ends low | the water that stayed is marked in the low place
samples: Two arrows from the hilltop down into the valley, and a mark where the water stayed. | An arrow drawn from the valley up the hill.

stem: Draw your tray from above, with the arrows and a key box.
answer: Two hills and a valley drawn from above, the arrows from the pour, the water where it stayed, and a key box saying what each mark means.
steps: draws the hills and the valley, not only the water | draws the arrows the pour made, high to low | fills in the key box so a partner could read each mark
samples: Two hills, a valley between them with water in it, arrows from the hill tops down, and a key box that says arrow = the water went this way. | Only a blue valley and some arrows, with no key box.

stem: Place the pieces on your paper to make a model of land and water. Draw the arrows and a key box.
answer: Hills, a hollow holding water, a river and the ocean placed on the paper, arrows on routes seen in the pour records, and a key box saying what each mark means.
steps: places the hills, the hollow with water, the river and the ocean | draws each arrow from high ground to lower ground | fills in the key box so a partner could read each mark
samples: Two hills, a hollow between them holding water, a river running to the ocean at the edge, arrows pointing down, and a key box. | A lake piece alone on bare paper with no hills, arrows or key.

stem: Change one thing on your model. Say it: I changed ___ because I saw ___.
answer: One change, and the pour record or picture that shows it, with the changed route running to lower ground.
steps: names a change | names the evidence, the pour record or a picture | the changed route runs to lower ground
samples: I changed the arrow to point down into the hollow because I saw it on our pour record. | I changed the colour because I like it.

stem: Look at the picture. Point the way that is lower.
answer: A point toward the low ground in the picture, where the puddle or the groove ends.
steps: points toward the lower ground, not the top of the picture | the support the child used is recorded on the scale: shown, shown with help, not yet seen
samples: Points toward the puddle at the low edge. | Points up toward the top of the page.

stem: Draw this corner from above. Show the way the water went, and add a key box.
answer: The garden bank and the grass drawn from above, one arrow along the groove from the bank to the grass, and a key box saying what the arrow means.
steps: draws the bank, the groove and the grass, not only the water | draws the arrow along the route the picture shows, high to low | fills in the key box so a partner could read the arrow
samples: A raised bank at the top, a groove running down to the grass, one arrow along the groove and a key box that says arrow = the water went this way. | A blue stripe with nothing round it and no key.

stem: Put your map beside your tray record. Say what is the same and what is different.
answer: One thing the two routes share, that the water ran from high ground to lower ground, and one thing that differs, such as the groove carrying it away where the tray gathered it.
steps: names one thing the two routes share | names one thing that differs | both come from the map and the tray record, not from guessing
samples: The same is the water ran downhill. The different is the tray water gathered in the valley and this water ran on along the groove. | The same is they are both pictures.

stem: Look at Stone Bay. Point to where the stream's water ends.
answer: The bay at the low edge of the picture, where the stream runs in.
steps: points to the bay, the low place | does not point up at the hills
samples: Points to the bay, where the stream stops. | Points to the top of a hill.

stem: Pip says that every river goes to the ocean. Look at Dry Ridge. Where does its stream end?
answer: In the lake, in the low place. There is no ocean on the Dry Ridge page, so Pip's words do not fit this picture.
steps: points to the lake | says there is no ocean on the page
samples: It ends in the lake, and there is no ocean here. | It goes to the ocean, because Pip said so.

stem: Change your model once, using Stone Bay or Dry Ridge. Draw the change.
answer: One change drawn from the new place, such as the bay or the lake with the land round it, with the water arrow running down to it and the key box filled in.
steps: draws the new water place with land round it, not the water alone | the arrow runs from higher land down to the low place | the key box says what each mark means
samples: The lake drawn in a low place with slopes round it, an arrow running down the gully to the lake, and a key box. | A blue lake alone, with an arrow running up the slope.

stem: Say the pattern. Water runs ___ and collects ___; the shapes here are ___.
answer: Water runs down and collects in a low place; the shapes here are a bay with low hills, or a lake with slopes all round it.
steps: says the water runs down or downhill | says it collects in a low place | names the shapes of the new place, which differ from the school
samples: Water runs down and collects in the bay; the shapes here are low hills and a beach. | Water runs up and collects on the hill; the shapes here are the same as our school.

stem: Look at the two chick pages. Point to one thing on each page that helps a young chick stay safe.
answer: On the first page the chick out of its shell, on the second the hen keeping the eggs warm, each with its caption.
steps: points to one detail on the first page | points to one detail on the second page | the caption is used for each, not a guess
samples: Points to the chick by its shell and to the hen on the nest, and reads each caption. | Points twice to the same page.

stem: The river story and the Water places map are both pages. Which one can tell us where water is?
answer: The Water places map, because its captions and key say where each water place is.
steps: chooses the map page, not the story | points to a caption or to the key as the reason
samples: The map. The key says the dot is a lake, and the caption says where. | The story, because it is nicer.

stem: Find the lake on the Water places map. Point to its dot and say what the key says.
answer: The filled dot beside the lake, which the key says means liquid water, and the caption says the lake lies in a low place left of the river.
steps: points to the dot beside the lake | reads the key for that dot | says the lake is liquid water
samples: Points to the filled dot, looks at the key, and says it means liquid water. | Says it is a lake because everyone knows, without the key.

stem: Circle each water place on your map. Draw its label.
answer: The ocean, river, lake and pond circled, each with a label, every one matched to its dot and the key.
steps: circles all four water places | each label comes from the caption or key | no hill or other land is circled
samples: Circles the ocean, river, lake and pond and labels each from its caption. | Circles the hills and leaves the pond.

stem: Hold both cups. Which cup holds solid water?
answer: The ice cup. The other cup holds liquid water.
steps: names the ice cup | the child has held both cups, not guessed
samples: The ice cup, it is hard and cold. | The water cup.

stem: Pip says the ice cup has no water in it. Tell Pip what you held.
answer: Ice is water that is solid. One cup held solid water and the other held liquid water, and both are water.
steps: says ice is water | says solid for the ice cup and liquid for the other | uses what was held
samples: I held ice and I held water. Ice is water that is solid. | Ice is not water, it is just ice.

stem: Find the snow on the Frozen water places map. Point to its dot and say what the key says.
answer: The open dot on the high peaks, which the key says means solid water.
steps: points to the dot on the snow | reads the key for the open dot | says solid
samples: Points to the open dot, checks the key, and says solid water. | Says the dot is filled because snow is water.

stem: Fill in your chart from both pages. Give at least four places, each with its page and its mark.
answer: At least four places from the two pages, each with its page name and the filled mark for liquid or the open mark for solid, with snow and ice marked solid.
steps: each place is on a page, not made up | each mark has its page name | liquid places have the filled mark and solid places the open mark | places come from both pages, not the story
samples: River, Water places, filled. Lake, Water places, filled. Snow, Frozen water places, open. Ice, Frozen water places, open. | River, Water places, filled. Pond, Water places, filled. Ocean, Water places, filled. River, filled.

stem: Look at two pictures of the ground under the swings. One is marked first month and one is marked last month, and the last-month picture has a scuffed hollow. The swing ground looked the same every day. Did it change? Point to yes or no.
answer: Yes. The two pictures are different: the last-month picture has a scuffed hollow that the first-month picture does not.
steps: points to yes | points to the scuffed hollow as the difference between the two pictures
samples: Yes. The last-month picture has a hollow and the first-month picture does not. | No, it looked the same every day.

stem: Look at two beach pictures, one marked before the storm and one marked after. The caption says: Storm waves carried the sand away in one night. Is this a fast change or a slow change? Point to the words that tell you.
answer: A fast change. The words in one night tell you.
steps: points to fast | points to the words in one night
samples: Fast. The words say in one night. | Slow, because erosion takes a long time.

stem: Look at two pictures of a sand pile at a building site, one before and one after. The caption says: The wind blew the top off the pile one afternoon. Is this fast or slow? Point to the words that tell you.
answer: Fast. The words one afternoon tell you.
steps: points to fast | points to the words one afternoon
samples: Fast. The words say one afternoon. | Slow, because wind and water wear things away slowly.

stem: Look at an older drawing of a flat ledge on a hillside terrace and a later drawing where the ledge has a rounded slope. The caption says: Rain splashed small bits down, a little each year. Nobody saw the ledge change on any day. Did it change? Point to yes or no.
answer: Yes. The later drawing is different from the older drawing: the flat ledge is now a rounded slope.
steps: points to yes | points to the rounded slope in the later drawing as the difference
samples: Yes. The later drawing has a rounded slope and the older one has a flat ledge. | No, because nobody saw it change.

stem: Look at two records of the Alder Creek bank. Record 1 shows an older view and a later view with the edge farther back, and says: a little each season. Record 2 shows a picture and says: after the flood a big piece was cut away in one night. Point to the record that shows the fast change.
answer: Record 2, the flood record, because its words say in one night.
steps: points to record 2 | points to the words in one night
samples: Record 2. It says in one night. | Neither, because erosion is always slow.

stem: A spray bottle wet a sand pile in a pan. Point to the card that shows what the pan cannot tell us. Card 1: which way the sand slides. Card 2: how long a real hillside takes to slide. Card 3: where the spray goes.
answer: Card 2: how long a real hillside takes to slide. A pan shows how sand moves, not how long a real change took.
steps: points to card 2, how long a real hillside takes to slide
samples: Card 2. The pan cannot show how long a real change took. | Card 1. The pan cannot tell us which way the sand slides.

stem: Look at two trays of damp sand with the same slope. Pip poured a small cup on one and a big cup on the other, and they lost different amounts. Does it matter that the cups were different sizes? Point to yes or no.
answer: Yes. The two trays must start the same (slope, how wet the sand is, size of cup), so the small-cup tray and the big-cup tray cannot be compared.
steps: points to yes | says or shows that the start (including the size of the cup) must be the same before pouring
samples: Yes. They did not start the same, so the amounts are not fair to compare. | No, because the slope was the same.

stem: The sand edge was at 0 on a ruler strip. After the pour it was at the second mark. How far did the edge move back? Write the number.
answer: 4 centimeters.
steps: starts the strip at 0 | reads the second mark to the whole centimeter
samples: 4 centimeters. | 5 centimeters, because I counted the marks.

stem: Look at three cards: a picture of a tall wooden fence, tray result bars for the fence and two other barriers, and a big close picture of the fence. Pip picks the fence because it looks strongest. Which card does Pip need before choosing? Point to it.
answer: The card with the tray result bars.
steps: points to the tray result bars | does not point to a picture of the fence
samples: The bars. They show how much each barrier lost. | The big picture, because it shows the fence best.

stem: Look at three cards: a tray with wood chips spread across the whole path, a bar showing the chips lost the least sand, and a tidy picture of the chips. The chips lost the least sand, and Pip says they have no weakness. Point to the card that shows something the chips might do poorly.
answer: The tray with the chips spread across the whole path, because the chips use up the path.
steps: points to the tray with chips across the whole path | says the chips use up the path
samples: The chips cover the whole path, so they use up the path. | The bar, because it says the chips lost the least.

stem: Look at a two-bar picture graph with one square for each centimeter and a limit line across both bars at 7. The mulch bar is 5 squares tall. The gravel bar is 9 squares tall. A limit is the most we allow. Which bar goes past the limit line? Point to it.
answer: The gravel bar, 9 squares, goes past the line at 7. The mulch bar, 5 squares, stays under the line.
steps: points to the gravel bar | reads the line at 7 as the most allowed
samples: The gravel bar. It is 9 and the line is at 7. | The mulch bar.

stem: Look at two pictures of the same garden strip: a curved screen and a staggered row of posts, each with wind blowing at it. Sketch both shapes, and draw an arrow for each to show how it turns the wind.
answer: Both shapes drawn, the curved screen and the staggered posts, each with a wind arrow that bends around or slows at the shape.
steps: draws the curved screen and the staggered row of posts | draws a wind arrow for each shape that bends around the shape or slows at it
samples: A curved screen with a wind arrow bending around it, and a row of posts set in a zigzag with a wind arrow slowing between them. | Only one shape is drawn, and the wind arrows run straight through both.

stem: Look at the same two pictures. How could we compare their protection fairly? Say it or point to a card.
answer: Use the same ground and the same fan place and the same conditions for both, then measure how much each lets the land retreat.
steps: says the ground, the fan place and the conditions must be the same | says to measure the retreat
samples: Same ground, same fan place, then measure the retreat of each. | Pick the one that looks stronger.

stem: Look at three cards: a row of tall cardboard tubes, bars from matched fan tests for the tubes and a flat board, and a close picture of the tubes. Pip says the tall tubes protect best. Which lost less sand, the tubes or the flat board? Point to a card and say the numbers.
answer: The flat board lost less: 3 and 3, against 6 and 7 for the tubes. The bars show it, not the look.
steps: points to the matched fan-test bars | says the flat board lost less, with its numbers (3 and 3 against 6 and 7)
samples: The flat board lost less, 3 and 3. The tubes lost 6 and 7. | The tubes, because they are tallest.

stem: Look at hedge H and fence F protecting the same dune strip, with a bar card. Hedge H lost 1 then 4 centimeters and uses 9 centimeters of path. Fence F lost 3 then 3 centimeters and uses 2 centimeters of path. The limits are: lose at most 5, and use at most 6 of the path. Which one meets both limits? Point to it.
answer: Fence F. It lost 3 and 3, which is 5 or less, and it uses 2, which is 6 or less. Hedge H uses 9 of the path, which is more than 6.
steps: points to fence F | says F is at or under both limits and H is over the path limit
samples: Fence F. It stays under both limits. | Hedge H, because it lost the least land at first.

stem: Look at four records. Two show a cliff losing a block, and their words say it came away in one storm. Two show a rocky surface growing smooth, and their words say it wore away little by little. Point to the two records for the fast change and the two records for the slow change.
answer: The two cliff records show the fast change, one storm. The two smoothing-surface records show the slow change, little by little. Each change has two sources and no numbers of years.
steps: points to both cliff records as fast, with the words one storm | points to both smoothing-surface records as slow, with the words little by little
samples: The cliff records are fast, they say one storm. The smooth rock records are slow, they say little by little. | The rocky surface is not changing, because it looks the same.

stem: Look at bars from equal water tests of three barriers, R, S and T. R lost 7 then 8 centimeters and uses 9 of the path. S lost 10 then 11 and uses 1. T lost 12 then 13 and uses 11. The limits are: lose at most 9, and use at most 10 of the path. Which barrier meets both limits? Point to it.
answer: Barrier R. It lost 7 and 8, which is 9 or less, and uses 9, which is 10 or less. S saves path but loses more than 9. T is over both limits.
steps: points to barrier R | checks both limits against the bars, not the look of the barrier
samples: R. It is under both limits. | S, because it looks the strongest.

stem: Barrier R lost 7 then 8 centimeters and uses 9 of the path. The limits are: lose at most 9, and use at most 10 of the path. Say one thing R does poorly.
answer: R uses 9 of the 10 centimeters of path it is allowed, which is almost all of the path.
steps: names a thing R does poorly, such as the path it uses | uses the bars, not how R looks
samples: R uses 9 of the path, almost all that is allowed. | R has no weakness because it protects better.

stem: Look at fresh wind tests of two barriers, X and Y, with the same limit: lose at most 6 each run. X lost 2 then 8 centimeters. Y lost 5 then 5. Which barrier would you choose? Point to it and mark both of its runs against the limit.
answer: Y. Both of Y's runs, 5 and 5, are at or under 6. X's second run, 8, is over 6.
steps: points to Y | marks Y's two runs, 5 and 5, as at or under the limit of 6
samples: Y. Both runs are under the line at 6. | X, because it lost the least the first time.

stem: Pick one piece in your new object made from the rocket. Tell us how its shape or the stiff card suits its job.

steps: names one piece and says how its shape or the stiff card suits its job
samples: The triangle is pointed, so it makes a roof, and the stiff card keeps its shape. | The card is stiff, but that does not matter for the job.

stem: Look at your card bus before you touch it. Draw it just as it is, with every piece in its place.
answer: A drawing of the bus as the teacher set it, with all five pieces in their real places.
steps: draws the original arrangement with all five pieces in their real places
samples: The drawing shows the bus with each of the five pieces where the teacher set it. | The drawing shows a different shape, or leaves pieces out.

stem: Take your card bus apart now. Lay the pieces out on the table.
answer: All five pieces lie separately on the table, so the bus is taken apart.
steps: separates all five pieces
samples: All five pieces are laid out one by one on the table. | The pieces stay stuck in the bus shape.

stem: Use exactly the five pieces of your bus to make a different object. Tell us what it is.
answer: A whole that is visibly different from the bus, made from all five pieces and no others.
steps: makes a visibly different whole from exactly the five pieces
samples: It is a robot now, made from all five pieces. | It is a smaller bus with only four pieces.

stem: Draw your new object. Show what changed from the bus.
answer: A drawing of the new whole that shows what changed, such as which circle moved or which rectangle now stands on its end.
steps: draws the new whole and shows what changed
samples: The drawing shows the new object and the piece that moved. | The drawing is the bus again.

stem: Draw a line from each piece in the bus to the same piece in your new object. Finish: The lines show ___.
answer: Five lines, one from each old piece to its place in the new object. The new object uses the same five pieces, so different objects can be made from one set.
steps: matches all five pieces by lines and says the new object uses the same pieces
samples: Five lines. It is the same five pieces in a new arrangement. | It is a new object, so it needs new pieces.

stem: Pick one piece in your new object made from the bus. Tell us how its shape or the stiff card suits its job.
answer: A named piece with a shape or stiffness reason, such as: the circle is round, so it makes a wheel; the stiff card keeps its shape.
steps: names one piece and says how its shape or the stiff card suits its job
samples: The circle is round, so it makes a wheel, and the stiff card keeps its shape. | The card is stiff, but that does not matter for the job.

stem: Look at the butter record. Solid butter. The butter melted and flowing after a grown-up heated it. The butter after it cooled, solid again in a different outline. Mark whether this change returned or remained, and say what shows it.
answer: Returned. After cooling the butter is solid again, though the outline is different.
steps: marks returned and uses the cooled, solid picture as the result of the attempted return
samples: Returned. We cooled it and it was solid again, in a different shape. | Remained, because the shape is different.

stem: Look at the butter record again. Say what the heat did to the butter.
answer: Heating changed the solid butter into a liquid.
steps: says that heating changed the butter from solid to liquid
samples: The heat made the solid butter flow. | The butter just changed by itself.

stem: Look at the cookie record. Soft dough. The dough baked into a firm cookie after a grown-up heated it. The cookie after it cooled, still a firm cookie. Mark whether this change returned or remained, and say what shows it.
answer: Remained. After cooling it is still a firm cookie and is not soft dough again.
steps: marks remained and uses the cooled, still firm cookie as the result of the attempted return
samples: Remained. We cooled it and it stayed a firm cookie. | Returned, because cooling takes it back to dough.

stem: Look at the cookie record again. Say what the heat did to the dough.
answer: Heating changed the soft dough into a firm cookie.
steps: says that heating changed the dough from soft to firm
samples: The heat made the soft dough firm. | The cookie was always firm.

stem: Look at the juice record. Liquid lemon juice. The juice after it was cooled until it froze. The juice after it was warmed until it flowed again. Mark whether this change returned or remained, and say what shows it.
answer: Returned. After warming the juice flows again as before.
steps: marks returned and uses the warmed, flowing picture as the result of the attempted return
samples: Returned. We warmed it and it flowed again. | Returned, because it froze.

stem: Look at the juice record again. Say what the cold did to the juice.
answer: Cooling changed the liquid juice into a solid.
steps: says that cooling changed the juice from liquid to solid
samples: The cold made the juice freeze solid. | The juice stayed liquid.

stem: Look at the cucumber record. A firm cucumber slice. The slice after it was frozen. The slice after it was warmed and thawed, still soft. Mark whether this change returned or remained, and say what shows it.
answer: Remained. After warming the slice is still soft and is not firm again.
steps: marks remained and uses the thawed, still soft slice as the result of the attempted return
samples: Remained. We thawed it and it stayed soft. | Returned, because cooling fixes it.

stem: Look at the cucumber record again. Say how the cold changed the cucumber, even after it thawed.
answer: Cooling changed the firm slice, so that it was soft after thawing.
steps: says that the cold changed the firm cucumber to soft
samples: The cold made the firm slice soft. | The cucumber did not change.

stem: Look at all four records. Tell us what heating and cooling can cause.
answer: Heating and cooling can cause some changes that go back, like the butter and the juice, and some that stay, like the cookie and the cucumber.
steps: says some changes go back and some stay
samples: Some changes go back, like the butter and the juice. Some stay, like the cookie and the cucumber. | Cooling always makes things go back to the start.

stem: Look at a different butter sample. Solid before, and melted after heating. There is no picture of it cooled. Is this enough to decide whether it returns? Say yes or no, and say what you need.
answer: No. We need to see what happens when it cools.
steps: says no | says it needs the cooled result, or a look after the temperature is changed back
samples: No. We need to see what it looks like after it cools. | Yes, it melted, so it will go back.

stem: Look at three pots of parsley with the same cups, the same soil and the same start. Pot P1 sits in the sun and is watered, and has new leaves. Pot P2 sits in the shade and is watered, and its leaves are falling. Pot P3 sits in the sun with no water, and it is drooping. Join two pairs of pots that make a fair test: one pair for light and one pair for water.
answer: P1 with P2 tests light, because only the light is different. P1 with P3 tests water, because only the water is different.
steps: joins P1 with P2 as the light test | joins P1 with P3 as the water test
samples: P1 with P2 for light, and P1 with P3 for water. | P2 with P3, because one is shaded and one has no water.

stem: Look at a lawn picture. A bucket lay upside down on the grass for a week. The picture shows the grass after the bucket was lifted. Say what you see.
answer: A round pale or yellow patch of grass where the bucket was, and green grass all around it.
steps: names the pale or yellow patch where the bucket was | names that the grass around it is green
samples: The grass under the bucket is pale, and the grass around it is green. | It is pale because it was too cold under the bucket.

stem: Look at three bean cups on a card dated February 6. All three have the same soil and start at 5 centimeters with two green upright leaves. Cup A is in the sun and gets two spoonfuls of water a day. Cup B is under a dark cover and gets no water. Cup C is in the sun and gets no water. Touch the one change that makes both tests with A fair: give B the same water as A, darken C, or change nothing.
answer: Give B the same water as A. Then B and A differ only in light, and C and A differ only in water.
steps: touches the change that gives B the same water as A
samples: Give B the same water as A, so B and A are different only in light. | Darken C, so two plants are in the dark.

stem: Look at the record card for bean cup C. It has the date, the sun with no water, and 5 centimeters. The leaf box and the stem box are empty. Draw what belongs in the leaf box and the stem box.
answer: Two green leaves in the leaf box and an upright stem in the stem box, the same as the starting records of A and B.
steps: draws two green leaves in the leaf box | draws an upright stem in the stem box
samples: Two green leaves and a straight stem drawn in the two boxes. | Says the height is enough and leaves the boxes empty.

stem: Look at the ruler photograph dated March 3. The soil is at zero and the top of the tomato plant is at 8 centimeters. It has three green upright leaves. It sits in the sun and is watered. Fill in this line of the dated table.
answer: March 3, sunlight with water, 8 centimeters, and three green upright leaves, drawn or labelled.
steps: writes the date, March 3 | names the condition, sunlight with water | writes 8 centimeters | draws or labels three green upright leaves
samples: March 3, sunlight with water, 8 centimeters, and a sketch of three green upright leaves. | 8 centimeters, and nothing else on the line.

stem: Look at two pairs of young sunflowers. In pair M, the cups, the soil and the water are the same, and one plant is in a bright window and one is in a dim corner. In pair N, the cups are different and the spoonfuls of water are different, and one plant is in a bright window and one is in a dim corner. Pip says the taller plant is the healthier one. Touch the pair that checks Pip's idea fairly.
answer: Pair M. Its cups, soil and water are the same, so only the light is different.
steps: touches pair M
samples: Pair M, because only the light is different. | Pair N, because one plant is in a bright window and one is in a dim corner.

stem: Look at a card of one sunflower that grew under a cover: it is tall and pale. Pip will look at it again next week. Touch the one thing that could show Pip's idea, that the taller plant is the healthier, is wrong. Its height, its colour and leaves, or the colour of its cup.
answer: Its colour and leaves. If the tall plant is still pale with thin leaves, taller is not healthier. Its height cannot show it, and the cup colour has nothing to do with it.
steps: touches the colour and leaves card | says that pale or thin leaves would show the tall plant is not healthy
samples: Its colour and leaves, because if it is still pale then tall does not mean healthy. | Its height, because taller means healthier.

stem: Look at two cards of a chive plant, dated May 2 and May 4. On May 2 the plant is 6 centimeters with three green upright leaves. On May 4 the same plant, kept in the dark and watered, is still 6 centimeters with three green upright leaves. Pip says the dark plant looks fine, so plants do not need light. Is Pip right yet? Say yes or not yet.
answer: Not yet. The dark plant looks fine today, so we keep recording before we say.
steps: says not yet | says to keep recording, or that it looks fine only so far
samples: Not yet. It looks fine today, so we keep watching it. | Yes, it looks fine, so plants do not need light.

stem: Look at two cards of a second chive plant, dated May 9 and May 11. On May 9 the plant is 7 centimeters with four green upright leaves. On May 11 the same plant, kept in the sun with no water, is still 7 centimeters with four green upright leaves. Pip says the sunlit plant looks fine with no water, so sunlight is all it needs. Is Pip right yet? Say yes or not yet.
answer: Not yet. The plant is standing up today, so we keep recording before we say.
steps: says not yet | says to keep recording, or that it is standing up only so far
samples: Not yet. It is standing up today, so we watch it until it changes. | Yes, it is standing up, so sunlight is all it needs.

stem: Look at the June 2 basil cards. The shaded basil is 10 centimeters tall with two pale leaves and a leaning stem. The sunlit basil is 7 centimeters with four green upright leaves. Pip says the shaded basil is healthier because it is taller. Touch the card that shows Pip is wrong: the ruler card, the leaves and stem card, or the pot card.
answer: The leaves and stem card: the shaded basil is pale and leaning, so being taller does not make it healthier.
steps: touches the leaves and stem card | says the pale leaves or the leaning stem, not the height
samples: The leaves and stem card, because the shaded plant is pale and leaning. | The ruler card, because it shows the shaded plant is taller.

stem: Look at four cards of a basil plant test with equal water. On June 2 the sunlit plant is 7 centimeters with four green upright leaves, and the shaded plant is 10 centimeters with two pale leaves and a leaning stem. The shaded plant is moved into the sun. On June 9 the first plant is 8 centimeters with five green leaves, and the moved plant is still 10 centimeters with four green leaves and a firmer stem. Did the moved plant get healthier? Say yes or no.
answer: Yes. It has more green leaves and a firmer stem, though its height did not change.
steps: says yes | names the green leaves or the firmer stem as the reason, not the height
samples: Yes. It has four green leaves now and a firmer stem. | No, because the height is the same.

stem: Look at three spinach plants. All started on April 1 at 3 centimeters with two green leaves. On April 15 the plant in the sun with water is 8 centimeters with four green leaves. The plant in the dark with water is 11 centimeters with two pale leaves. The plant in the sun with no water is 3 centimeters with two wilted leaves. Touch the two pairs that test light and water fairly.
answer: The sun with water beside the dark with water, and the sun with water beside the sun with no water.
steps: touches the sun with water beside the dark with water | touches the sun with water beside the sun with no water
samples: Sun with water beside dark with water, and sun with water beside sun with no water. | Dark with water beside sun with no water.

stem: Look at the same spinach plants. Tell us what in each fair pair shows what a plant needs.
answer: In the light pair, the dark plant is taller but pale, so a plant needs light. In the water pair, the dry plant wilted and did not grow, so a plant needs water. Both support needing light and water for healthy growth.
steps: says the dark plant is taller but pale, so it needs light | says the dry plant wilted with no gain, so it needs water
samples: The dark plant is taller but pale, and the dry plant wilted and did not grow. | The dark one is taller, so it is healthier.

stem: Look at two lettuce seedlings that started the same size. Plant L sits in a sunny window and is watered every day. Plant M sits in a closet and gets no water. Pip says L and M show that light matters. Touch the two things that are different between L and M.
answer: The light and the water.
steps: touches the light | touches the water
samples: The light and the water. | Only the light.

stem: Look at the same lettuce seedlings L and M, and three more plants: a watered plant in the closet, a plant in the window with no water, and a second plant just like M. Touch the plant we could add to compare with L for light alone.
answer: The watered plant in the closet. It differs from L only in light.
steps: touches the watered plant in the closet
samples: The watered plant in the closet, because only the light is different. | A second plant just like M.

stem: Look at two nasturtium plants. The left plant is 17 centimeters tall, pale and leaning, with two thin leaves. The right plant is 12 centimeters tall, green and firm, with four leaves. Touch the healthier plant.
answer: The shorter plant on the right.
steps: touches the shorter, green plant
samples: The right plant, the shorter one. | The left plant, because it is taller.

stem: Look at the same two nasturtium plants. Touch what tells you which plant is healthier.
answer: The leaf colour, the number of leaves, or the stem, and not the height.
steps: touches the leaf colour, the number of leaves or the stem, not the height
samples: The green leaves and the firm stem. | The height.

stem: Look at two cards of a mustard plant that was watered every day and kept in a closet. On Day 1 it is green. On Day 12 it is pale and limp. Pip says water is all a plant needs. Touch the picture that tells whether Pip is right.
answer: The Day 12 picture. The watered plant in the dark is pale and limp, so water is not all it needs.
steps: touches the Day 12 picture
samples: The Day 12 picture, because it is pale and limp. | Pip is right.

stem: Look at two pepper plants in a sunny window. One has had no water and is limp. The other is watered and green. Pip says sun is all a plant needs. Touch the picture that tells whether Pip is right.
answer: The limp plant. It had sun but no water, so sun is not all it needs.
steps: touches the limp plant
samples: The limp plant, because it had sun and no water. | Pip is right.

stem: Read your class plant at the soil. Put the zero of the ruler where the soil is, and tell us how tall the plant is to the whole centimeter.
answer: The ruler's zero is at the soil, and the height is read to the nearest whole centimeter.
steps: puts the ruler's zero at the soil | reads the height to the whole centimeter
samples: I put zero at the soil and read the top of the plant at a whole centimeter. | I stood the ruler on the rim of the cup.

stem: Fill in your dated observation table for this plant: the date, the condition, the height and how the plant looks.
answer: A line with today's date, the condition (sunlight with water, dark with water, or sunlight with no water), the height in whole centimeters, and the leaves and stem drawn or labelled.
steps: writes today's date | names the condition | writes the height in whole centimeters | draws or labels the leaves and the stem
samples: A dated line with the condition, a whole-centimeter height, and a sketch of the leaves and the stem. | A height and nothing else.

stem: Tell us which plant your plant is compared with, and the one thing that is different between them.
answer: Each missing-factor plant is compared with the healthy plant, and the one difference is light for the dark plant or water for the dry plant. A child reading the healthy plant says it is compared with the dark plant for light or the dry plant for water.
steps: names the healthy plant as the plant to compare with (a child reading the healthy plant names the dark or dry plant) | says the one thing that is different, light or water
samples: My dry plant is compared with the healthy plant, and only the water is different. | My dark plant is compared with the dry plant.

stem: Use your day 52 record. Draw one bar for each of the three plants on your graph sheet, and write the condition under each bar.
answer: Three bars standing on the shared zero line, one square for each centimeter, with sun with water, dark with water and sun with no water written under them.
steps: draws the bars up from the shared zero line | uses one square for each centimeter | writes the three condition labels under the bars
samples: Three bars from the zero line, one square for each centimeter, each with its label. | Bars that start at different heights, with no labels.

stem: Box 1. Look at the puppet stage with plants P and Q. P is tall and pale. Q wilted. What could each plant be missing?
answer: Missing light could explain P, and missing water could explain Q.
steps: names missing light as a possible cause for P and missing water as a possible cause for Q
samples: P may lack light, and Q may lack water. | P is tall, so the dark place is the best.

stem: Box 2. The caretaker says comparing P with Q proves which place is better. Why can we not tell from P and Q alone?
answer: P and Q differ in two things at once, light and water, so we cannot tell which one caused each change.
steps: says P and Q differ in two things at once, light and water
samples: P and Q are different in light and in water, so it is not a fair test. | P and Q are a fair test, so the sunny place is better.

stem: Box 3. Draw one more plant that you add to finish the test.
answer: A matching plant in the sun that gets two spoonfuls of water every day, the healthy plant.
steps: adds a matching plant in the sun with water
samples: A plant in the sun with two spoonfuls of water a day. | A plant in the dark with no water.

stem: Box 4. Draw lines to show which two plants you compare for light, and which two you compare for water.
answer: A line from P to the added plant for light, and a line from Q to the added plant for water, each by itself.
steps: compares P with the added plant for light and Q with the added plant for water, each by itself
samples: A line from P to the added plant, and a line from Q to the added plant. | A line from P to Q.

stem: Box 5. Draw or write what stays the same for all the plants.
answer: The kind of plant, the starting size, the cups, the soil, the room temperature and the days you look.
steps: names at least four things kept alike: kind, starting size, cups, soil, temperature, days you look
samples: Same kind, same cups, same soil and same room. | The plants are in the sun.

stem: Box 6. Show how much water each plant gets.
answer: The added plant and P get two spoonfuls every day, the same on the same days, and Q gets none.
steps: gives the added plant and P the same water on the same schedule, and Q none
samples: Two spoonfuls every day for the added plant and P, and none for Q. | Three spoonfuls for P and two for the added plant.

stem: Box 7. Show when you will measure the plants.
answer: Measure each plant's height from the soil on the same dates, again and again for two weeks.
steps: plans height measurements more than once, on dated days
samples: I will measure all of them every few days for two weeks and write the dates. | I will measure once at the end.

stem: Box 8. Show what else you will look at besides height.
answer: The leaves, their colour and how many, and the stem.
steps: includes the leaves and the stem or condition beside height
samples: The colour and number of the leaves, and the stem. | Only the height, because the tallest wins.

stem: Measure your class plant once more. Fill in the last line of your record: the date, the condition, the height and how the plant looks.
answer: A dated line with the condition, a height read with zero at the soil to the whole centimeter, and the leaves and stem drawn or labelled.
steps: puts the ruler's zero at the soil and reads whole centimeters | enters the date and the condition | enters the height | draws or labels the leaves and the stem
samples: A last line with the date, the condition, a whole-centimeter height and a sketch of leaves and stem. | A height and nothing else.

stem: Look at your record from day 52. Say or write what you did with your plant and what you recorded.
answer: A first-person account of the child's own procedure and dated record, such as: I measured our watered dark plant from the soil. Today it is 11 centimeters, pale and leaning. I compare it with our watered sunlight plant.
steps: follows the agreed condition and measurement procedure | makes an identifiable dated height and appearance record
samples: I measured our watered dark plant from the soil. Today it is 11 centimeters, pale and leaning. I compare it with our watered sunlight plant. | Our group measured the plants, and I do not know which one.

stem: Look at the later records after fourteen days: the sun-and-water plant, and P. They have the same water. Tell us what the comparison shows about light.
answer: The two plants differ only in light. P, with no light, is taller but pale, with a weak stem, so a plant needs light to grow healthy.
steps: names the sun-and-water plant against P as the light comparison | says P is taller but pale and weak, so a plant needs light to grow healthy
samples: They are different only in light. P is taller but pale and weak, so a plant needs light. | P is the tallest, so the dark is the best place.

stem: Look at the later records after fourteen days: the sun-and-water plant, and Q. They have the same light. Tell us what the comparison shows about water.
answer: The two plants differ only in water. Q, with no water, stayed small and wilted, so a plant needs water to grow healthy.
steps: names the sun-and-water plant against Q as the water comparison | says Q stayed small and wilted, so a plant needs water to grow
samples: They are different only in water. Q did not grow and wilted, so a plant needs water. | Q was in the sun, so a plant does not need water.

stem: Look at the card of a fly standing on one flower with yellow powder on its legs, beside a second flower. Touch what the yellow powder is: pollen or a seed.
answer: Pollen. It is pollen, and pollen is not a seed.
steps: says or touches pollen
samples: Pollen, because it is the yellow powder on the fly. | A seed.

stem: Draw an arrow for where the powder can go next.
answer: An arrow from the fly to the second flower.
steps: draws an arrow that starts at the fly | ends the arrow at the second flower
samples: An arrow from the fly's legs to the second flower. | An arrow that stops halfway, or none.

stem: Look at a card seed that keeps sliding off a smooth plastic mitten model. Touch what to change: swap in fuzzy cloth where the seed touches, or paint the mitten red.
answer: Swap in fuzzy cloth where the seed touches, so the hooks have something to catch.
steps: touches swap in fuzzy cloth
samples: Swap in fuzzy cloth, so the hooks can catch. | Paint the mitten red.

stem: Look at a paper bird on a string that flaps its wings when you pull. Say or draw one thing this paper bird model cannot show.
answer: Anything the model leaves out: how a real bird really flies, how heavy it is, or what it eats.
steps: names one thing the model cannot show: how a real bird flies, its weight, or what it eats
samples: It cannot show how a real bird flies. | Nothing, it shows everything.

stem: Look at the ruler picture. Zero is at the taped line. A card seed rode on a felt strip and stopped with its edge at one mark. Read where the edge stops, to the whole centimeter.
answer: 17 centimeters.
steps: reads from the zero mark at the taped line | reads the edge to the whole centimeter, 17
samples: 17 centimeters, reading from zero. | 18 centimeters, counting the zero mark as 1.

stem: Look at the records. A hooked seed falls from bare card and stays on fuzzy cloth. A smooth seed falls from both. Touch the sentence the records support: every seed sticks to fuzzy cloth, or only the hooked seed stuck.
answer: Only the hooked seed stuck.
steps: touches only the hooked seed stuck
samples: Only the hooked seed stuck, and the smooth seed fell. | Every seed sticks to fuzzy cloth.

stem: Say or draw one thing these records cannot tell us.
answer: Any true limit of the stick-or-fall records, such as whether the seed would grow, how far it moved, or what a real animal does.
steps: names one true thing the records cannot tell, such as growing, how far a seed moved or what a real animal does
samples: They cannot tell us if the seed would grow. | They tell us everything about seeds.

stem: Look at a model moth that carries yellow dots from one flower. The second flower's patch never touches them. Touch the part to move so the dots can be left there: the receiving patch, the moth's wings, or swap the dots for seeds.
answer: The receiving patch, moved so it touches the dots the moth carries.
steps: touches the receiving patch
samples: The receiving patch, so it touches the dots. | The moth's wings.

stem: Why did the moth go to the flower? Touch food, or to help the plant.
answer: Food. The yellow powder that stuck on the way may be left on the next flower.
steps: touches food
samples: Food, and the powder sticks on the way. | To help the plant.

stem: Look at your jay model. Show the part that stands for the jay's beak.
answer: The folded-card halves, which stand for the beak.
steps: shows the folded-card halves as the beak
samples: These folded-card halves are the beak. | The feathers I drew on the card.

stem: Show the part of your model that stands for the oak, the plant.
answer: The plant outline, where the acorn starts.
steps: shows the plant outline as the oak
samples: This outline is the oak, and the acorn starts here. | The leaf litter is the oak.

stem: Show what your model carries, and say what it stands for.
answer: The large card acorn. It stands for the acorn, which is a seed.
steps: shows the card acorn as what is carried | says it stands for an acorn, a seed
samples: This card is an acorn, a seed from the oak. | It carries pollen.

stem: Look at your drawing. Draw a line from each part of your model to the real part it stands for.
answer: A line from the card halves to the jay's beak, from the card acorn to the acorn, and from the outline to the oak.
steps: joins the card halves to the beak | joins the card acorn to the acorn
samples: Lines from the card halves to the beak, from the card acorn to the acorn and from the outline to the oak. | Lines that go to the picture of the jay as a whole, with no parts named.

stem: Show where your model's route starts.
answer: At the plant outline, where the acorn lies.
steps: starts the route at the plant outline where the acorn lies
samples: It starts here at the oak outline, where the acorn is. | It starts in the leaf litter.

stem: Show how your model carries the acorn.
answer: The beak halves close around the card acorn and hold it while the model moves.
steps: closes the beak halves around the card acorn | moves the model with the acorn held
samples: The card halves close on the acorn and I move them with the acorn held. | My pretty jay need not carry anything.

stem: Show where your model leaves the acorn.
answer: The beak halves open over the paper leaf litter, away from the plant outline, and the acorn stays there.
steps: opens the beak halves over the leaf litter | leaves the acorn away from the plant outline
samples: I open the halves over the leaf litter, away from the oak, and the acorn stays. | The acorn stays at the oak.

stem: Tell how the beak halves hold the acorn and let it go.
answer: Closing the halves holds the acorn and opening them lets it go. The beak is the part that holds, so hooks are not needed.
steps: says closing holds the acorn | says opening lets it go
samples: Closing the halves holds the acorn and opening them lets it go. | The acorn has hooks and sticks to the beak.

stem: Look at your trial record. Tell one change you made after your first try because of what it showed, or one part you kept because it worked.
answer: A change made because of what the trial showed, such as folding the sides more after the acorn slipped, or a reason to keep a part that worked.
steps: says what the first trial showed | gives a change that follows from it, or a reason to keep a working part
samples: I folded the sides more because the acorn slipped. | I changed it because it looked nicer.

stem: Tell one thing your model cannot show.
answer: Whether the acorn would grow, or what a real jay does, such as eating. Paper cannot eat.
steps: names one thing the model cannot show
samples: It cannot show if the acorn would grow. | The model shows everything the jay does.
